summary:
ASEAN Flood Watch is an interactive flood-risk research platform covering 46 study areas across 11 Southeast Asian countries. It combines NASA POWER rainfall data with open weather, soil-moisture, elevation, and local geographic information to produce a transparent educational risk index. Users can explore locations on a detailed map, compare source-data risk ranges, and test how heavier rainfall could change conditions through an interactive storm scenario.

The project addresses the challenge by turning complex Earth-observation data into information that students, families, and communities can understand. Every indicator explains its source, weight, limitations, and missing data instead of presenting the result as an official forecast.

This matters because monsoon flooding affects communities across national borders, while useful environmental data is often fragmented or difficult to interpret. ASEAN Flood Watch demonstrates how accessible technology and NASA data can support regional awareness, encourage further research, and help young people understand the environmental risks facing their communities.
details:
What the project does

ASEAN Flood Watch is an interactive flood-risk research platform covering 46 study areas across 11 Southeast Asian countries. Users first select a country and then a city, basin, or flood-prone region. The map displays the study area, its risk colour, and a numerical risk range.

The platform has two modes:

  • Source Data uses current stored environmental data and displays a risk interval.
  • Storm Scenario lets users explore how heavier rainfall could change the risk score.

The educational risk index combines five factors:

  • Future rainfall: 35%
  • Previous rainfall: 25%
  • Soil moisture: 20%
  • Low-elevation exposure: 10%
  • River rise: 10%

NASA POWER provides historical precipitation estimates. Open-Meteo supplies forecast rainfall, modelled surface soil moisture, and elevation metadata. When river-level observations are unavailable, the platform keeps that factor missing and shows a bounded score range instead of silently treating it as zero.

Benefits and intended impact

Flooding is a shared problem across Southeast Asia, especially during monsoon seasons. However, environmental data is often spread across different platforms and can be difficult for students and families to understand.

ASEAN Flood Watch turns complex datasets into an accessible visual experience. It helps users:

  • Identify environmental conditions associated with flooding.
  • Compare flood-risk factors across countries.
  • Understand how rainfall, soil moisture, terrain, and rivers interact.
  • Explore possible storm conditions without presenting them as official predictions.
  • Access linked original data and learn where each value comes from.

The intended impact is educational awareness. We want young people to see that Earth-observation data can help communities understand real-world problems. The project could also serve as a foundation for future work using local river gauges, drainage data, historical flood events, satellite flood maps, and official warning thresholds.

Tools and technologies

The website was developed with:

  • HTML5
  • CSS
  • Vanilla JavaScript
  • Node.js for data-refresh scripts and automated tests
  • Leaflet for interactive mapping
  • MapLibre GL JS for detailed vector-map rendering
  • OpenFreeMap and OpenStreetMap for geographic context
  • NASA POWER Daily API for precipitation data
  • Open-Meteo APIs for forecasts, soil moisture, and elevation
  • OSRM road geometry for illustrative route scenarios in Hue and Hoi An
  • Git and GitHub for version control
  • GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for automatic deployment

No special hardware is required. The project runs in a modern web browser and is designed to work on ordinary computers and tablets.

What makes it creative

The project expands a local Vietnam flood concept into a cross-border ASEAN research platform while keeping each location connected to its own geography and flood type. It combines a regional overview with detailed city-level exploration and allows users to move between observed-source conditions and interactive storm scenarios.

A particularly important design choice is the treatment of missing data. Instead of inventing a value, the system displays a risk interval and clearly explains what information is missing. Every dataset includes its source, original request link, retrieval time, and limitations.

Factors considered by the team

We considered monsoon rainfall, river flooding, urban drainage, coastal exposure, flash floods, terrain, soil saturation, data availability, and differences between countries. We also considered the limits of point-based data, delayed satellite estimates, missing river gauges, and the difference between an educational index and a validated flood forecast.

For safety and scientific honesty, the platform does not claim to provide flood probabilities, official warnings, verified evacuation routes, or street-level predictions. It is a transparent student research prototype intended to encourage learning, discussion, and further validation.
